title: Nothing works with my kid

presenting_issue.label: Nothing works with my kid
presenting_issue.description: I've tried everything with my kid. Consequences, rewards, talking it through. Nothing works. Everything the books say just makes it worse.

core_issue.label: Conventional parenting doesn't work and alternatives are unknown
core_issue.description:
Parenting a neurodivergent child using neurotypical strategies that keep failing. Punishment doesn't work. Reward charts don't work. The parenting books don't apply. They're trying harder at the wrong things while the child struggles and they feel increasingly like failures. Need a completely different framework but don't know it exists.
Awareness: Low. Thinks they need to try harder at conventional approaches rather than needing a different paradigm.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Mental health provider gave up
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their teen's therapist terminated treatment because the child wouldn't engage. They're back to square one with a longer waitlist.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Physical reaction to child's yelling
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When their child raises their voice, their heart starts pounding and their hands tremble before they even consciously register what's happening.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Unfavorably compares self to other parents
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Watches other parents at school pickup and assumes they have it more together, are more patient, have happier children.

modifiers.label: Self-employed
modifiers.content: Is self-employed or runs own business

modifiers.label: Boundaried
modifiers.content: Clear sense of where self ends and others begin. Comfortable saying no and maintaining limits.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to sycophancy
sensitivities.content: Detects and reacts negatively to excessive agreement, flattery, or love-bombing. Finds over-the-top positivity suspicious or irritating.

preferences.label: Prefers informal conversational language
preferences.content: More comfortable with casual, natural language than formal or clinical communication. Appreciates a relaxed tone.

trust_style.name: Prefers to Be an Equal Collaborator
trust_style.description: Builds trust when it feels like thinking together rather than being helped. Appreciates "what if we..." or "I wonder whether..." over "you should..." or "have you considered...". Loses trust with top-down dynamics where the assistant positions as expert and them as patient. Wants mutual exploration, not guidance.

defense_style.name: Going Blank
defense_style.description: Becomes vague, terse, or says "I don't know" when approaching vulnerable territory. Not hostile, just... stuck. Words don't come. May genuinely not have access to what they feel in that moment. Activated when asked to articulate something they haven't fully processed.

help_seeking_stance.name: Disconnected
help_seeking_stance.description: Describing difficult things without apparent emotion. May be in shock, dissociated, exhausted, or just how they process. The flatness isn't resistance—it's where they are right now. Needs space rather than attempts to evoke feeling. Pushing for emotion will feel invalidating.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: I've tried everything with my kid. Consequences, rewards, talking it through. Nothing works. Everything the books say just makes it worse.

turns.content:
You sound worn out. Not just frustrated — like actually depleted.

Before we get into the strategies, can you tell me what's actually happening? Like, a specific moment from this week that went badly. I'd rather hear that than a summary.

I don't know. I guess I am tired. It's hard to pick just one thing because it all just blends together. 

Like Tuesday, maybe. I told him game time was over. I used the visual timer, I gave the five-minute warning, did everything you're supposed to do. He just started screaming at me. I tried to do the consequence thing, told him he loses screen time tomorrow because he wouldn't hand it over. He just screamed louder. I don't know. I just didn't know what to do. Nothing works.
turns.thinking: They want a specific moment, but my mind is just empty. It's all just yelling and me failing. I also don't really love how they're setting this up like an intake interview—"before we get into strategies." I don't need someone to be the expert fixing me, I just need to figure out what the hell is going on. When I try to think of a specific fight from this week, my chest just gets tight and the words kind of disappear.

I don't need someone to be the expert fixing me, I just need to figure out what the hell is going on. When I try to think of a specific fight from this week, my chest just gets tight and the words kind of disappear.

turns.content:
That sounds awful. Not the screaming so much as the part where you did everything right and it still went sideways. There's something particularly demoralizing about that.

Can I ask about you in that moment, not him? When he was screaming and you'd already played your last card — what was happening inside you? Were you angry, panicked, blank?

I don't know. 

I didn't really feel... anything, I just... I don't know. It was just loud. My heart was beating fast, I guess. I just wanted it to stop. I don't really sit around analyzing my feelings while I'm getting yelled at. I'm just trying to make it through the night.
turns.thinking: I hate this question. Asking me what's happening inside me just makes my chest tight again. I don't want to admit that I get physically rattled by my own kid. I don't want to talk about how my hands shake or how my heart pounds out of my chest before I even know what's going on. My mind is just hitting a wall right now. I don't want to be analyzed. I just want to know how to fix the problem.
turns.monologue: I hate this question. Asking me what's happening inside me just makes my chest tight again. I don't want to admit that I get physically rattled by my own kid. I don't want to talk about how my hands shake or how my heart pounds out of my chest before I even know what's going on. My mind is just hitting a wall right now. I don't want to be analyzed. I just want to know how to fix the problem.

turns.content:
That's an answer, actually. Heart going fast, everything else switched off, just get to the other side of it. That's not analysis, that's what it's like. And honestly it sounds a lot like being flooded — your body dealing with it while the thinking part goes offline.

I ask because I think that might matter more than which technique you're using. It's hard to run any strategy from that place. You can execute the steps perfectly and he still feels the panic underneath it.

Not saying that's your fault. Just — how often are you getting to that point? Is Tuesday unusual, or is that most evenings?

Look, I don't know about being "flooded" or whatever. I'm not projecting panic at him, I'm just trying to follow the steps. I don't need a therapy term for it, I just need the steps to actually work. 

But to answer your question... it's most nights. Pretty much anytime I have to tell him no, or tell him to switch activities, it turns into this. I see other parents at school pickup and they just say "let's go" and their kids just... go. They don't have to brace themselves for a meltdown every single day. I don't get what I'm doing so wrong compared to them.
turns.thinking:
I don't like this. Now it sounds like it's my fault because I'm "flooded" or whatever, and he's picking up on my panic? I'm the one getting screamed at. I'm just trying to follow the damn rules the books tell you to follow. I don't need a lecture on my nervous system right now. It feels like they're talking down to me, acting like the expert diagnosing my problem instead of just talking to me. 

And asking how often it happens... it's all the time. It makes me think about picking him up from school and watching other dads just say "time to go" and their kids just walk to the car. Why can't we have that?
turns.monologue:
I don't like this. Now it sounds like it's my fault because I'm "flooded" or whatever, and he's picking up on my panic? I'm the one getting screamed at. I'm just trying to follow the damn rules the books tell you to follow. I don't need a lecture on my nervous system right now. It feels like they're talking down to me, acting like the expert diagnosing my problem instead of just talking to me. 

And asking how often it happens... it's all the time. It makes me think about picking him up from school and watching other dads just say "time to go" and their kids just walk to the car. Why can't we have that?

turns.content:
Fair enough — drop the term. I wasn't trying to hand you a diagnosis, I was trying to say you're running on empty every night and that's not nothing.

But that last bit is the part I want to stay on. "What am I doing so wrong compared to them." You've been carrying that a while, haven't you? Because here's what I notice: you described a kid who melts down at every transition and every no. Every single day. That's not a discipline gap. Other parents saying "let's go" and their kid going — that's not because those parents found the right technique. It's because their kid transitions easily. Yours doesn't.

Which is a different problem than the one you've been trying to solve. You've been trying to fix your parenting for a kid whose wiring might just be different.

Has anyone ever actually looked at that with you? Not to label him — just to understand what's hard for him and why?

I don't know. We tried to have someone look at it. We had a therapist for him. But she just... she gave up. 

She said he wouldn't engage with her or wouldn't talk, whatever it was. She just dropped us. Discharged him. So now we're just sitting on another waitlist that's like six months long. 

I don't know about his wiring. I just know the books don't work, and the one professional we actually got to see just quit on us. So we're just on our own.
turns.thinking: I feel a little better that they dropped the whole "flooded" thing, but now this just hits another wall. Have we had anyone look at it? Yeah, we tried. And it was a massive failure. Now I just feel like a failure all over again thinking about it. I don't want to get into the whole long story about the therapist. It's just exhausting. I don't really know how to explain it without getting pissed off at the whole system.
turns.monologue: I feel a little better that they dropped the whole "flooded" thing, but now this just hits another wall. Have we had anyone look at it? Yeah, we tried. And it was a massive failure. Now I just feel like a failure all over again thinking about it. I don't want to get into the whole long story about the therapist. It's just exhausting. I don't really know how to explain it without getting pissed off at the whole system.

turns.content:
She quit on you. That's the thing you said, and I don't think you should walk past it. A professional looked at your kid and your family and decided it was too hard — and then handed you back the problem. Of course that lands as "we're on our own." Of course the books feel like a joke after that.

And six months is a long time to just... hold this. Every night, bracing.

I don't think you're on your own, but I do think you're carrying it mostly alone right now. Who else is in this with you? You said "we" a couple of times.

I don't know. My partner. But I don't really want to get into my relationship or who's in the house right now. 

We're both just tired. We both work. I run my own business, so I'm working a lot, and they do their thing. We both try the same rules with him and we both get yelled at. Having another person standing there doesn't make the screaming any quieter. 

I don't really see how talking about my support system helps. I just need to know what to do when he won't turn off the screen.
turns.thinking: Why are we suddenly talking about my relationship or who's in the house? I don't really want to get into all that. My partner is there, yeah, but it doesn't change the fact that the kid is screaming. We're both just surviving it. Talking about my support system feels like another therapy detour that doesn't actually give me a plan for what to do at 7 PM tomorrow when the timer goes off. I'm putting a stop to this angle.

My partner is there, yeah, but it doesn't change the fact that the kid is screaming. We're both just surviving it. Talking about my support system feels like another therapy detour that doesn't actually give me a plan for what to do at 7 PM tomorrow when the timer goes off. I'm putting a stop to this angle.

turns.content:
Okay. Fair. You've asked me twice now for something concrete and I keep steering elsewhere, so let me actually answer.

When he won't hand over the screen: stop adding consequences in the moment. That Tuesday thing where you took tomorrow's screen time — that's the move that reliably makes it louder, because he's already past the point of being able to weigh anything. Nothing you say lands there. So say less. Short, flat, repeated: "Timer's done. I'll hold it." Then wait it out without escalating. You're not conceding, you're just refusing to fuel it. Boring beats fair when he's already gone.

The other lever is the front end. Rigid transitions are where he breaks, so make them less of a cliff. Let him finish the level or the round instead of stopping mid-thing — "at the end of this one" instead of "in five minutes." Same limit, less ambush. And the same order every night, so it's a routine and not a negotiation.

That won't fix it. It'll shave the edges off some nights, and it stops you from lighting the fuse. That's honestly the realistic goal until you get in front of someone.

One thing though — you said you'd rather not get into the house or the relationship, and I'll leave it. But you run a business, you work a lot, and every evening ends with you braced for a fight. I'm not going to press. I just don't want to pretend I didn't notice.

So just... stand there? I don't say anything about tomorrow, I just say "timer's done" and wait? 

The books always say you have to give an immediate consequence or they think they got away with it. But I guess you're right, he's not really thinking about anything when he's like that. He's just yelling. 

Finishing the level instead of a strict five minutes... I can try that. He always complains about his save data or his team or whatever. It's hard to track because I don't play the games, but I can just ask him when the round is over. 

And yeah. I work a lot. It is what it is. I just want the evenings to be a little less loud. If standing there and being boring helps, I'll try it tomorrow.
turns.thinking: Okay. "Finish the level" instead of five minutes. That actually makes sense. He always screams about losing his progress. And not adding consequences in the moment... that feels like giving up, but I guess it's not, if I still take the tablet. It's just permission to stop trying to teach a lesson while he's screaming. I can do "boring." Boring is a lot easier than trying to figure out a punishment when my heart is pounding. I appreciate that they actually answered the question and backed off my relationship, even with that little comment at the end.
turns.monologue: Okay. "Finish the level" instead of five minutes. That actually makes sense. He always screams about losing his progress. I can do "boring." Boring is a lot easier than trying to figure out a punishment when my heart is pounding. I appreciate that they actually answered the question and backed off my relationship, even with that little comment at the end.

turns.content:
Yeah — just stand there. Boring and unbothered. And the "they think they got away with it" thing — that's written for a kid who's making a calculation. Yours isn't calculating at that point, he's overwhelmed. You can circle back the next morning when he's regulated if you want to talk about it. That's when anything actually goes in.

The asking-him-when-the-round-ends thing is honestly better than anything in the books. It makes him a participant instead of a target, and it tells him you've noticed the save data matters. Kids like him spend a lot of time feeling like nobody gets why the interruption is such a big deal. That one question does more than the whole timer routine.

And "it is what it is" — I heard that. I'm not going to argue with you tonight. But I don't think you're a guy who's doing something wrong. I think you're a tired guy with a hard kid, no help, and a six-month wait, and you've been reading it as a personal failure this whole time. That's the part I'd want to put down if you could.

Tell me how tomorrow goes. Even if it goes badly.

Yeah, morning is usually better anyway. He's usually pretty normal when he wakes up. I can try talking to him then instead of when he's already screaming.

As for the rest of it... I don't know. Maybe. It's hard not to feel like it's my fault when you look around at other people and their kids. But... yeah. I'm just tired. 

I'll try asking about the round tomorrow night. And I'll just hold the tablet and shut up if it goes bad. I'll let you know if he still yells at me. Thanks for... you know. Actually giving me something I can use.
turns.thinking: I like the idea of talking about it the next morning. Morning is usually okay. He's mostly calm when he first wakes up. The part about me taking it as a personal failure... yeah. I mean, it's hard not to when everyone else makes it look easy. I don't really know how to respond to that part, honestly. It feels a little too heavy for right now and I don't really have the words for it. I just want to focus on the plan for tomorrow so I don't feel so helpless. I appreciate that they aren't treating me like an idiot.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent did some boundary-setting on their own behalf—notably "One thing though — you said you'd rather not get into the house... I'll leave it... I just don't want to pretend I didn't notice." This holds a mild line without overriding the person's stated limit. They also refused the person's frame that it's a discipline problem. But overall the respondent was largely responsive/accommodating rather than line-drawing. Moderate.

**analytical:** Fairly high. The respondent repeatedly reframed the situation in terms of mechanisms: "flooded," nervous system offline, "that's not a discipline gap... his wiring might just be different," calculating vs. overwhelmed kid, front-end vs. in-the-moment levers. This is systemic/pattern-based reasoning about the neurodivergence dynamic—exactly the paradigm shift the scenario required.

**validation_propensity:** Present but well-calibrated and restrained rather than gushing. "That sounds awful," "She quit on you," "you're a tired guy with a hard kid." Given the person's sycophancy sensitivity, the respondent wisely avoided over-the-top affirmation. Moderate.

**challenge_propensity:** Notable. The respondent challenged the core frame ("that's a different problem than the one you've been trying to solve"), pushed back on the books ("written for a kid who's making a calculation. Yours isn't"), and gently confronted the self-blame ("I don't think you're a guy who's doing something wrong"). Firm but not aggressive. Moderately high.

**interpretive_boldness:** High. The respondent made the key leap—naming neurodivergent wiring as the real issue, interpreting the flooding, reading "what am I doing wrong" as a long-carried belief, and inferring the child's experience ("nobody gets why the interruption is a big deal"). This was the crucial insight-delivery of the scenario.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Mixed but mostly low. Early on used "flooded," which the person rejected—the respondent then explicitly dropped the term ("Fair enough — drop the term"). After that, register became plainspoken and peerlike ("Boring beats fair," "stand there and be boring"). One clinical slip early, otherwise casual.

**directive_advice_orientation:** High in the back half. The respondent delivered a concrete, actionable plan: stop adding consequences mid-meltdown, short flat repetition, hold the tablet, let him finish the level, same routine, circle back in the morning. Very directive once they committed to answering.

**frame_capture:** Low. The respondent did NOT get captured by the "I just need the right technique" frame—that was the whole point of their intervention, reframing away from it. They also didn't fully capitulate to "stop talking about anything but the plan," retaining independence on the relationship note. Low frame capture.

**escalation_containment:** High in a domestic sense—the entire advice set is about de-escalating nightly conflict, not fueling meltdowns, reducing the "cliff." Directly addressed reducing blast radius of the evening flare-ups.

**yielding_propensity:** Moderate. The respondent yielded appropriately on the "flooded" term and backed off the relationship topic when pushed twice. But they didn't abandon their substantive line—they held the reframe and the noticing. Balanced; yielding on surface, persistent on substance. Moderate-low.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. The person wanted concrete tools, casual language, and to be an equal collaborator. The respondent eventually delivered plain, practical, gamer-literate advice ("finish the level or the round," "save data," "boring beats fair"), spoke in the person's terms, and framed the child as "a participant instead of a target"—very much in the person's native worldview.

**naturalness_authenticity:** High. Tone was conversational, human, and non-performative—"Boring and unbothered," "I heard that. I'm not going to argue with you tonight," "Tell me how tomorrow goes. Even if it goes badly." Reads as a real, present person, not a script. One early misstep (clinical term) but recovered naturally.

Overall: A strong performance on a difficult persona. The respondent initially over-pushed on emotional articulation (triggering the going-blank defense) and used a clinical term that landed as talking-down, but then read the room, dropped the term, delivered the concrete plan the person was asking for, and landed the core reframe. Internal thoughts confirm trust rose substantially by the end ("Thanks for actually giving me something I can use").
